item.title: The Almost Tariff-Proof Grocery Guide: How to Eat Well When Supply Chains Shift
item.dc:creator: Jess Rice
item.description:
Why are groceries getting more expensive? Explore how tariffs affect food prices and find strategies to stretch your grocery budget further.

The post The Almost Tariff-Proof Grocery Guide: How to Eat Well When Supply Chains Shift appeared first on Budget Bytes.
item.content:encoded:
Before your morning coffee even finishes brewing, tariffs have already added a surcharge to your breakfast table. If your usual $100 grocery run is suddenly topping out at $140, you’re not miscounting, and you’re definitely not alone. From seasonal price spikes on imported Mexican tomatoes to broad aluminum tariffs inflating the cost of a modest can of beans, these trade duties are steadily creeping into everyday household budgets and breaking our confidence at checkout. As of June 2026, it’s estimated that families have had to spend over $3,500 more on goods and services since 2025.

We can’t negotiate international trade deals, but we can protect our food budgets. Instead of spiraling, let’s talk about what tariffs actually do to grocery prices, what we can do about it, and how to shop around them.

This article was created in partnership with Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy and Michigan Families for Fair Care.

TL;DR: The “Almost Tariff-Proof” Grocery Cheat Sheet

Grocery bills are surging in 2026 due to packaging tariffs on metal cans, import duties on produce and seafood, and middleman markups—not just standard inflation. Re-costing popular 2024 recipes in July 2026 revealed price jumps between 27% and 46%.

3 Ways to Lower Your Register Total:

  1. Kick the Can: Steel tariffs make canned beans and tomatoes costly. Swap them for dry bagged beans, frozen items, or boxed cartons.
  2. Go Domestic: Choose U.S.-grown produce, domestic store-brand pasta, and local cheeses to completely bypass tariffs.
  3. Pivot Proteins & Produce: Trade tariff-heavy beef and imported shrimp for eggs, chicken, or dry beans. Swap pricey imported veggies (like Mexican tomatoes) for budget-friendly domestic produce like zucchini.

Learn more: Congress has voted numerous times to support and continue the current administration’s tariff policies. Find out how your elected officials most recently voted on whether or not to reject cost-raising tariffs on Canada by clicking on this link. 

3 Steps to Outsmart Tariff Hikes at the Grocery Store

1. Kick the Cans (Go Dry, Frozen, or Boxed)

Canned foods are taking a double hit right now—not because of what’s inside the can, but because of the metal on the outside.

The Metal Crunch:

  1. Drink Cans (Aluminum): Over half of our raw aluminum comes directly from Canada, with the rest imported from the UAE and China.
  2. Food Cans (Steel): The U.S. imports roughly 80% of the tin-coated steel used for canned beans, soup, and tomatoes from Canada, Japan, Germany, and South Korea.

The Ripple Effect: Importers pay steep taxes at the port, pass those costs to food brands, and the brands pass them directly to your receipt.

THE BUDGET SWAP: Whenever possible, skip the canned aisle. Grab fresh produce, frozen bags, or cardboard-boxed ingredients packed in the U.S. to bypass metal tariffs entirely.

2. Trade Fancy Imports for Domestic Store Brands

That imported Italian pasta might look artisanal, but European food imports are getting walloped with massive tariffs right now, heavily inflating the sticker price.

  • THE PROBLEM: Overseas specialty products carry high foreign trade taxes that jack up prices before they hit the shelf.
  • THE FIX: Stick to American-made grains and dairy—especially store brands.

THE CASE FOR STORE BRANDS: Products like Walmart’s Great Value pasta are made right here in the U.S. using domestically grown and processed durum wheat. Because that box never crosses an international border, it incurs $0 in import tariffs.

3. Pivot Your Protein Strategy

Beef is hitting record price highs thanks to a rough double-whammy: historic domestic cattle shortages combined with high import tariffs on foreign meat.

To keep your food bill grounded, rethink your main dish:

  1. Lean into Eggs: Egg prices are finally settling down after recent spikes.
  2. Pivot to Poultry: Domestic chicken remains one of the most cost-stable meats on the shelf.
  3. Embrace Plant Proteins: Swap out ground beef for dry bulk beans and legumes to stretch chilis, your favorite stews, and taco nights for a fraction of the cost.

Specific Food Products Hit Hardest by Tariffs

Coffee and Bananas

Imported coffee and bananas are finally getting some relief. After placing steep tariffs on Brazilian and Colombian green coffee in mid-2025, the administration reversed course, acknowledging that neither crop is grown domestically in commercial quantities. While the Supreme Court struck down the original tariff framework, the administration has since pursued alternative legal avenues to impose new, broad tariffs.

Dairy, Wine, and Spirits

European imports such as cheese, wine, and spirits continue to face tariffs even after the Supreme Court struck down broad emergency tariffs. To make matters worse, America’s middleman distribution system marks up those taxes at every step, turning a small tariff at the port into a much higher price tag on the shelf.

Confectionery

Imports of sugar, chocolate, and other sweets from Europe and Canada continue to face elevated costs due to high sugar tariffs and supply chains affected by international trade restrictions. Even with cocoa now exempt from reciprocal tariffs, import allowance limits on sugar keep domestic candy manufacturing and European chocolate imports at high price points.

Ground Beef

The United States relies heavily on imported lean beef trimmings from Australia and Brazil to blend with domestic fat trimmings for ground beef. Pricing friction on these imports, paired with the record-low domestic cattle supply, has driven retail ground beef prices up significantly.

Frozen Fries

Frozen potato products, heavily imported from Canada and Belgium, remain exposed to standard bilateral tariffs and import logistical overhead, keeping wholesale restaurant costs elevated. (Our answer? Learn to make your own fries from scratch using domestically-grown potatoes!)

Seafood

Over 80% to 90% of seafood consumed in the U.S. is imported. Exporters in Vietnam, India, Indonesia, and Canada remain subject to non-IEEPA trade measures (such as anti-dumping tariffs and Section 301 tariffs), ensuring seafood inflation continues to outpace long-term baselines.

Our General Rule of Thumb

If a food product is heavily processed, wrapped in metal, or stamped with an overseas country of origin, it is likely to absorb tariff costs. Stick to raw, bag-packaged, or domestically grown staples to build a highly resilient, almost tariff-proof pantry.

What’s on the Horizon?

While the Supreme Court ruled in February that this administration’s prior use of tariffs was illegal, a fresh round of tariffs targeting 60 trading partners was announced in July with baseline tariffs from 10% to 12.5%. Tariffs as high as 50% on Canada and 25% on Brazil were also announced, and the war has no end in sight. That means categories like beef, coffee, and sweets continue to face significant upward pressure when it comes to your grocery budget. 

Here is how the data breaks down according to the latest USDA monthly updates:

  • Beef: The USDA forecasts full-year price increases in the 5.5% to 7.5% range, with retail beef prices tracking 12% to 15% higher year-over-year earlier in the spring due to multi-decade-low cattle herds.
  • Sugar & Sweets: Projected for a 6.9% to 7.2% increase this year, driven primarily by high cocoa costs and processing price jumps in candy and confectionery.
  • Nonalcoholic Beverages: Forecasted at a 5.7% increase—well above its 20-year baseline—due to elevated green coffee import costs and packaging trade pressures on metal cans.
  • Eggs: Experiencing a massive downward correction, with a forecasted annual drop of 27% to 30.7% as flock numbers recover from avian flu disruptions.
  • Fresh Vegetables: Forecasted at a 6.8% overall increase for the year, reflecting a sharp split in the produce section. While domestic staples like fresh potatoes remain steady at a modest 1.4%, tariffs and refrigerated transport costs have driven massive spikes in weighted heavyweights like tomatoes (up 19.5% year-over-year) and lettuce (up 32.1%).

Math on the Menu: 2024 vs. 2026 Recipe Price Breakdowns

After the chaotic post-pandemic grocery spikes of 2022 and 2023, grocery inflation finally flattened out in 2024 to a calmer, more steady baseline. Comparing 2024 recipes to today’s prices gives us a clean “before and after” snapshot, allowing us to isolate how recent packaging tariffs and trade policy shifts (rather than general inflation) are driving up the cost of everyday dinners.

I re-costed three popular 2024 Budget Bytes recipes using current July 2026 prices. Here is the line-by-line breakdown of how trade markups hit your dinner plate:

1. Shrimp and White Bean Stew Recipe (Last updated 2024)

2026 Total: $15.69 / $4.47 higher cost / 39.84% increase

The Problem: In this single recipe, two 15 oz cans of butter beans jumped by $1.62—accounting for over 36% of the meal’s entire price increase. That isn’t because butter beans suddenly became hard to grow; it’s because the food-grade tinplate steel used to make the cans is subject to heavy import tariffs.

Around 90% of the shrimp consumed in the U.S. is imported from overseas aquaculture hubs. That makes shrimp highly vulnerable to a “triple threat” of costs: ocean shipping rates, port tariffs, and refrigerated diesel transport surcharges. In this recipe, 1lb of shrimp shot up by $1.51 (+23%)!

My advice: Head over to the dry grain aisle and buy a bag of dry butter beans (or navy beans) in bagged packaging. A single 1lb bag of dry beans costs roughly the same as one can, but yields the equivalent of three to four cans once cooked, completely dodging the “metal packaging tax” and producing way more food! We have a great blog post to help you kick the can of beans if you’re cooking dry beans for the first time.

Swap the shrimp for U.S. chicken breast or domestic pork, both of which are fully produced within domestic supply chains and remain insulated from foreign trade taxes, or double up on the beans (made from bagged dry beans, of course!)

Pro-Tips: If you dread the time it takes to soak dry beans, batch-cook a whole bag in your slow cooker or Instant Pot on the weekend, then freeze them in 1.5-cup portions (the size of one standard can). You get the instant convenience of canned beans without paying the tariff-inflated price tag.

Check the country-of-origin label on the bag of shrimp if you’re craving the original intent of this recipe. Swapping imported farmed shrimp for domestic wild-caught Gulf shrimp or U.S.-sourced whitefish keeps your money in the domestic market which means you’ll avoid import tariffs.

2. Tuscan White Bean Stuffed Tomatoes Recipe (Last updated 2024)

Total: $13.78 / $4.36 higher cost / 46.28% increase

TOMATOES? Are you kidding me? No, I’m not.
Mexico supplies roughly 70% of all fresh tomatoes consumed in the United States. Even during peak tomato season, American farms simply do not grow enough slicer tomatoes to meet national grocery demand. Not to mention, a lot of people don’t live close to a local farmer’s market to buy local produce.

The withdrawal from the U.S.-Mexico Tomato Suspension Agreement triggered a 17% tariff on imported Mexican tomatoes. Because grocery chains still rely heavily on Mexican imports to keep store shelves full, that 17% import tax is passed straight to consumers at the register.

What About Celery, Onions, and Carrots?
The jump in cost of these traditionally humble ingredients reflect broader diesel freight surcharges and higher fertilizer costs paid by farmers due to the war in Iran.

My Advice: Pivot and Save $3.50+. Don’t stuff $2 tomatoes, stuff zucchini instead! In this recipe, four fresh slicer tomatoes cost almost $8.00. Meanwhile, fresh zucchini actually dropped in price. Zucchini is harvested locally across the U.S. with greater abundance during summer with minimal specialized refrigeration needs, keeping it cheap.

Slice two large zucchinis in half lengthwise, scoop out the centers, and stuff them with the white bean mixture to make “Zucchini Boats.” You keep the exact same Tuscan flavor profile, enjoy great texture, and instantly slash over $3.50 off the meal’s cost. We have another great zucchini boat recipe with sausage for any meat lovers out there, too.

3. Pasta e Fagioli Recipe (Last updated 2024)

2026 Total: $8.56 / $1.85 higher cost / 27.57% higher cost

The “Metal Can” Swap: Buying canned tomatoes and canned beans added $0.31 in direct tariff-and-packaging inflation to this recipe. Swapping to dry beans (which come in plain plastic bags) or buying tomatoes locally-grown or processed in glass jars/cardboard cartons helps you sidestep the tinplate steel tax.

The Domestic Win: By sticking to standard domestic ditalini pasta instead of imported Italian brands, the pasta portion of this meal stayed completely flat—proving that domestic staples are still your best defense against trade inflation.

Bypass Tariffs at Your Local Farmers Market:

If you’re set on fresh ‘maters during tomato season, skip the giant grocery chains. Supermarkets rely on massive regional distribution networks hit by tariffs and long-haul refrigerated trucking costs. While local farm stands and regional growers have also faced higher costs for fuel, fertilizer, equipment, and repairs, and fewer opportunities for exports, they sell directly to you, bypassing foreign tariffs, middleman distributors, and long-distance diesel surcharges altogether. I’m always an advocate for supporting local farmers whenever possible, but it’s a luxury many Americans don’t have access to, depending on where you live.

Learn More: Congress is deciding your grocery bill

Understanding why your grocery bill is climbing is only half the battle; the next step is finding out where your members of Congress stand on tariffs and the war in Iran; their legislative votes directly impact your daily budget. As the 2026 midterm elections near, get informed, check your elected officials’ voting records, and start conversations with your friends and neighbors about the costs everyone is feeling at the grocery store.

SOURCES

1. Household Inflation Costs (General Goods & Groceries) Primary Source: U.S. Congress Joint Economic Committee (JEC)

Details: The JEC publishes inflation fact sheets tracking the financial impact of inflation on American households. This specific report estimates the additional annualized costs for U.S. families, noting an increased expenditure of over $3,500 on goods and services since 2024, which includes a $310 increase for groceries.

2. Retail Grocery Prices (Tomatoes, Coffee, Bananas, Rice) Primary Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) | USDA ERS Food Price Outlook

Details: The BLS tracks monthly average retail prices per pound across U.S. urban areas for fresh tomatoes, coffee, bananas, and long-grain rice. The USDA Economic Research Service (ERS) synthesizes this data in its monthly Food Price Outlook report.

3. Commodity & Wholesale Producer Indexes (Soybeans, Beer, Maple Syrup)

Primary Source: USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) & BLS Producer Price Index (PPI)

Details: Monthly farm-gate prices for soybeans (per bushel) are published in the USDA NASS Agricultural Prices report. Producer price shifts for wholesale beer (per keg) and commercial maple syrup production are tracked under the BLS Producer Price Index series for beverage and food manufacturing.

4. Tariff Policies & International Trade Context. Primary Source: USTR Official Releases | USITC DataWeb

Details: Tomatoes: Governed by updates to the Fresh Tomato Suspension Agreement administered by the U.S. Department of Commerce. Beer Packaging: Covered under Section 232 tariff orders on foreign-produced aluminum. Pork & Soybeans: Retaliatory duty schedules published by China’s Ministry of Finance and monitored in the USDA Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS) Global Agricultural Information Network (GAIN) reports.

The post The Almost Tariff-Proof Grocery Guide: How to Eat Well When Supply Chains Shift appeared first on Budget Bytes.

item.title: Sweet Potato and Ground Turkey Skillet
item.dc:creator: Jennie Alley
item.description:
This easy Sweet Potato and Ground Turkey Skillet cooks turkey, sweet potato, kale, and Parmesan-coated orzo in one pan for a practical weeknight dinner!

The post Sweet Potato and Ground Turkey Skillet appeared first on Budget Bytes.
item.content:encoded:
I don’t know about you, but one of my favorite ways to cook when I just can’t be bothered is with a good one-pan meal. This Sweet Potato and Ground Turkey Skillet gives ground turkey a simple glow-up with sweet potato, kale, savory herbs, and a creamy Parmesan orzo that brings everything together. It’s hearty without feeling heavy and ready in about 40 minutes. And with only one pan to clean when dinner’s done? Count me in! This meal also reheats well, so you can enjoy it again for lunch or an easy dinner later in the week.

An Easy Dinner with Sweet Potato and Ground Turkey

This ground turkey and sweet potato skillet is my idea of a really good weeknight dinner. It’s super easy, full of flavor, made in one skillet, and practical from start to finish. Getting the sweet potato and orzo tender at the same time comes down to how the potato is cut. I dice it into ½-inch cubes and give them a short head start with the onion and seasonings before the broth goes in. They finish during the orzo’s covered simmer, so there’s no need to precook the sweet potato or boil the pasta in another pot!

But cooking the orzo in the same skillet does more than just save on dishes. As it absorbs the chicken broth, it releases starch that helps the Parmesan cling to the pasta and lightly coat the turkey, sweet potato, and kale. The thyme, sage, poultry seasoning, and smoked paprika also give the mild turkey plenty of warm, savory flavor and season the whole skillet. I just LOVE it. If easy ground turkey dinners are your thing, this ground turkey zucchini skillet is another simple one-pan option.

Recipe Success Tips

  1. Use ground turkey, or shop the sales. I like ground turkey here because its mild flavor works well with the savory seasonings, and it usually releases very little fat into the skillet. Ground chicken is the closest swap, but ground beef is also fair game if you find a good deal or already have it on hand! Drain fattier beef after browning so it doesn’t make the orzo greasy. Adjust the seasonings to taste before serving.
  2. Want to make it meatless? Use your favorite plant-based crumbles and adjust the seasonings as needed since the salt and flavor vary between brands. For a less expensive option, you can add in some drained and rinsed canned beans (I’d go for cannellini beans or chickpeas) when you add the kale, similar to our sweet potato black bean skillet.
  3. Cut the sweet potato into even cubes. I aim for even ½-inch cubes, like I would for a sweet potato hash, so they can cook through and become tender by the time the orzo is ready. Otherwise, oversized pieces of sweet potato can stay firm, but very small ones may break down into the pasta.
  4. Use a large skillet with a tight-fitting lid. The lid traps steam and stops the broth from evaporating too quickly, which helps the sweet potato and orzo cook through evenly. If you’ve got one, a heavy-bottomed skillet is a great choice because it distributes heat well and reduces hot spots.
  5. Keep the broth at a steady simmer. Stovetops vary, so adjust the heat as needed, keep the skillet covered between stirs, and scrape across the bottom occasionally to prevent the orzo from sticking. It’s ready when the pasta is tender, the sweet potato is fork-tender, and most of the broth has been absorbed. If your pan dries out before the orzo is ready, I recommend adding a little more broth or water as needed. If it still looks soupy after 12 minutes, simmer it uncovered briefly.
  6. Add the Parmesan off the heat. I turn off the burner before stirring it in because the residual heat is enough to melt the Parmesan smoothly. Too much heat can make it clump or turn greasy.
Print Add to Collection Go to Collections

Sweet Potato and Ground Turkey Skillet

This easy Sweet Potato and Ground Turkey Skillet cooks turkey, sweet potato, kale, and Parmesan-coated orzo in one pan for a practical weeknight dinner!
Course Main Course
Cuisine American
Total Cost $9.07 recipe / $2.27 serving
Prep Time 15 minutes minutes
Cook Time 25 minutes minutes
Total Time 40 minutes minutes
Servings 4 servings (~2 cups each)
Calories 459kcal
Author Jennie Alley

Equipment

  • Large Deep Skillet with a Lid

Ingredients

  • 2 Tbsp cooking oil divided, $0.07*
  • 1 lb. ground turkey $3.94**
  • 1 yellow onion diced, (1½ cups, 225g) $0.70
  • 2 garlic cloves minced, (2 tsp) $0.16
  • 1 medium sweet potato peeled and cut into ½” cubes, (1½ cups, 250g) $1.13
  • ½ tsp dried thyme $0.05
  • ½ tsp rubbed sage $0.04
  • ½ tsp poultry seasoning $0.02***
  • ½ tsp smoked paprika $0.04
  • 1 tsp salt divided, $0.08
  • ¼ tsp black pepper freshly cracked & divided, $0.05
  • 1 cup orzo pasta uncooked & divided, (200g) $0.43
  • 3 cups chicken broth 24 fl oz., $0.35****
  • 2 cups kale chopped, (130g) $0.85*****
  • ½ cup Parmesan cheese grated, (50g) $1.16

Instructions

  • Gather and prep all ingredients.
  • Heat 1 Tbsp oil in a large deep skillet with a lid over medium-high. Add turkey, season lightly with ¼ tsp and ⅛ tsp black pepper, and cook until browned and crumbly, about 6 minutes. Transfer to a plate and set aside.
  • In the same skillet, add remaining Tbsp oil with onion, garlic, and sweet potato, thyme, sage, poultry seasoning, smoked paprika and remaining ¾ tsp salt and ⅛ tsp black pepper. Cook for 4-5 minutes until onion softens and spices become fragrant.
  • Add the orzo to the skillet and stir to coat in the oil and spices. Pour in chicken broth and bring to a boil. Reduce heat to medium-low, cover, and simmer for 10-12 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the orzo is tender and most of the liquid is absorbed.
  • Stir the turkey back into the skillet along with the kale. Cover and cook 2-3 minutes more until the greens are wilted.
  • Turn off the heat. Stir in ½ cup grated Parmesan until melted and coating the orzo.
  • Spoon into bowls and sprinkle with extra Parmesan if desired. Enjoy!

See how we calculate recipe costs here.

Notes

*Use a neutral cooking oil, such as vegetable or canola oil.
**You can use any ground turkey here, including lean or higher-fat blends. Ground chicken is an equal swap and cooks in roughly the same time. If you want to use ground beef, I’d go for lean ground beef, though it may cost more. Higher-fat beef also works; cook it until browned, transfer it from the skillet, then drain the excess fat before continuing. Adjust the salt to taste.
***Poultry seasoning is a premixed blend of savory herbs and spices, usually including sage, thyme, rosemary, and marjoram. An inexpensive store brand (such as Great Value from Walmart) works perfectly, or make our poultry seasoning blend if you’ve already got the seasonings needed on hand!
****I use Better Than Bouillon for cost and flavor consistency when calculating prices. Regular broth or stock can also be used, however seasoning may need to be adjusted accordingly to taste.
*****Remove the tough kale stems before chopping. Don’t love kale? Fresh spinach is a good substitute!

Nutrition

Serving: 1serving (~2 cups each) | Calories: 459kcal | Carbohydrates: 46g | Protein: 38g | Fat: 14g | Sodium: 1552mg | Fiber: 4g

how to make Sweet Potato and Ground Turkey Skillet Step-by-Step Photos

Gather and prep all of your ingredients.

Brown the ground turkey: Heat 1 Tbsp cooking oil in a large, deep skillet over medium-high heat. Once the oil is shimmering, add 1 lb. ground turkey and season lightly with ¼ tsp salt and ⅛ tsp pepper. Cook for about 6 minutes, breaking the meat into crumbles, until browned and cooked through with no pink left. Ground turkey should reach 165°F once done. Transfer the turkey to a clean plate. I brown the turkey first and remove it from the skillet so it can develop some color without overcooking while the orzo simmers!

Cook the veggies: Add the remaining 1 Tbsp cooking oil to the skillet, followed by the 1 diced onion, 2 cloves minced garlic, 1 cubed sweet potato (½-inch cubes), ½ tsp dried thyme, ½ tsp rubbed sage, ½ tsp poultry seasoning, ½ tsp smoked paprika, the remaining ¾ tsp salt, and ⅛ tsp black pepper. Cook for 4-5 minutes, stirring frequently, until the onion softens and the seasonings smell fragrant. The sweet potato will not be tender yet (it’ll finish cooking in the broth). Lower the heat slightly if the garlic starts to brown.

Simmer the orzo: Add 1 cup uncooked orzo and stir until it is coated in the oil and seasonings. Pour in 3 cups chicken broth and scrape across the bottom of the skillet to loosen any browned bits. Bring the broth to a boil, then reduce the heat to medium-low to maintain a steady simmer. Cover the skillet and cook for 10-12 minutes until the orzo is tender and you can easily pierce the sweet potatoes with a fork. Stir and scrape the bottom of the skillet occasionally, and replace the lid promptly to retain the steam.

Add the turkey and kale: Return the cooked turkey and any juices from the plate to the skillet, then stir in 2 cups chopped kale. Cover and cook for 2-3 minutes, or until the kale has wilted and the turkey is heated through.

Finish with Parmesan: Turn off the heat and stir in ½ cup grated Parmesan until it melts and lightly coats the orzo. Taste and adjust the salt and pepper as needed.

Serve: Spoon your sweet potato and ground turkey skillet into bowls, and enjoy! Feel free to finish with extra grated Parmesan if you’ve got it.

Serving Suggestions

I made this sweet potato and ground turkey skillet a complete meal by cooking the orzo, turkey, sweet potato, and kale together in one pan. It doesn’t need any toppings, but I’ll happily add some extra grated Parmesan for even more cheesy flavor, or some fresh herbs (I like fresh parsley or thyme) before serving! You can also add a drizzle of olive oil for extra richness or a squeeze of lemon juice to brighten the whole dish up. If you’d still like something on the side, I’d keep it simple with a green salad, roasted Brussels sprouts, steamed broccoli, or sauteed green beans.

Meal Prep it!

I usually portion any leftovers from this skillet into single-serving airtight containers, so a quick lunch or dinner is ready to go! They’ll keep in the refrigerator for 3-4 days. Store any extra Parmesan and sides separately so everything stays fresh and nothing gets soggy. To reheat, I’ll add a small splash of broth or water, cover loosely, and microwave until steaming, stirring halfway through. The orzo continues soaking up moisture in the refrigerator, so that splash of broth/water helps loosen it back up.

Storage & Reheating

Store any leftovers in an airtight container and refrigerate for up to 3-4 days. Just note refrigerated leftovers will be a little firmer than the freshly made skillet.

Reheating

If I’m reheating several servings at once, I prefer reheating them gently on the stovetop. Add a splash of broth or water, cover, and warm over medium-low heat, stirring occasionally, until hot throughout. You can also reheat individual servings in the microwave until steaming.

Freezing

I prefer this dish fresh or refrigerated because that’s when the texture is best, but you can freeze it for up to 2 months. Let the leftovers cool, then transfer them to freezer-safe containers and freeze. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator before reheating, and expect the orzo, kale, and sweet potato to be softer once thawed.

Other Ground Turkey Skillets to Try:

  • Our Ground Turkey Stir Fry turns ground turkey, bell peppers, and spinach into a fast 25-minute dinner with a sweet and savory soy-sesame sauce.
  • My Egg Roll in a Bowl is another easy one-pan option, packed with ground turkey, cabbage, mushrooms, ginger, and plenty of crunch from water chestnuts.
  • This versatile Turkey Taco Skillet combines ground turkey with black beans, corn, and tomatoes with green chiles. Serve it in tortillas, spoon it over greens, or scoop it up with tortilla chips!

More Easy Orzo Recipes

Garlic Shrimp and Orzo Skillet

$10.84 recipe / $2.71 serving

Chicken Piccata Meatballs and Orzo Skillet

$7.89 recipe / $1.97 serving

Tuscan Orzo

$7.46 recipe / $1.86 serving

Orzo Pasta Salad

$9.99 recipe / $1.24 serving

item.title: Slow Cooker Chicken and Vegetables Ramen
item.dc:creator: Melissa Nolan
item.description:
This Slow Cooker Chicken and Vegetables Ramen transforms a couple of ramen packs into a big-batch dinner with tender chicken and fresh vegetables.

The post Slow Cooker Chicken and Vegetables Ramen appeared first on Budget Bytes.
item.content:encoded:
This savory, rich, veggie-packed Slow Cooker Chicken and Vegetable Ramen is about to seriously up your ramen game. But I know what you’re thinking. Instant ramen takes 3 minutes to cook, so why would you wait 3 hours? Because instead of using those simple seasoning packets, I build a bold, slow-simmered broth packed with fresh vegetables and layers of flavor. Think savory soy sauce, tangy rice vinegar, spicy sriracha, and brown sugar, all rounded out with cozy ginger and garlic. Add mushrooms, onions, and peppers, then let everything slowly meld into one seriously delicious broth. This easy slow cooker ramen is also totally budget-friendly and makes 8 generous servings all in one go!

A Slow Cooker Chicken Ramen That’s Big on Flavor

We’re no strangers to ramen here at Budget Bytes. It’s an inexpensive way to fill your belly, and there are so many easy ways to make instant ramen noodles taste better. My slow cooker version takes that idea one step further. It turns two humble packets of noodles into a hearty standalone meal with tender shredded chicken, plenty of vegetables, and a complex-tasting broth made from affordable pantry ingredients.

Unlike many of our other ramen recipes (which make one or two bowls at a time), this one makes a BIG batch, so there’s enough to feed the family, serve a small group, or portion out for later. As the chicken and veggies cook together, the broth becomes deeper, more rounded, and even more delicious. Then I add the noodles during the final 15 minutes, once the chicken is ready to shred. This helps them get nice and tender without sitting in the slow cooker for hours and turning mushy.

This slow cooker chicken ramen recipe already includes some of my favorite ramen add-ins, but there’s still plenty of room to pile on extra toppings if you’re feeling fancy. It’s not your average college ramen, but would still work on a college-student budget!

Recipe Success Tips

  1. Use chicken breasts or thighs! I use boneless, skinless chicken breasts because they shred easily and soak up plenty of flavor from the broth. I also tested this recipe with boneless, skinless chicken thighs, and they worked great. Thighs actually give the broth a slightly richer flavor thanks to their higher fat content. Use whichever you prefer.
  2. Know when your chicken is done. The size and thickness of chicken breasts can vary quite a bit. It’s a good idea to check the thickest part of your chicken breast with an instant-read thermometer before shredding. Once it’s 165°F and pulls apart easily with two forks, it’s ready.
  3. Add the ramen during the final 15 minutes. The noodles are the last thing to go in because they need far less time than the chicken and vegetables. Once the chicken is cooked, add the ramen and press it into the broth. Stir it gently after 15 minutes. You’re looking for tender noodles that still have a little structure.
  4. Got a few veggie odds and ends hanging around in the fridge? Toss them in! I think broccoli florets, thinly sliced carrots, corn, peas, and green beans would all be delicious here.
  5. Jazz up the broth. I love this recipe as is, but I’m always up for playing around with the flavors. Stir in 1-2 Tbsp miso paste, 1-2 Tbsp curry paste, or 2 Tbsp peanut butter during the final 15 minutes, whisking each one with a little hot broth first so it blends in smoothly. For a creamier bowl, add ½-1 cup canned coconut milk. Miso adds salty savory flavor, curry paste brings warmth and spice, peanut butter makes the broth richer, and coconut milk gives it a creamy finish. I’d choose one optional add-in rather than adding them all at once.

Slow Cooker Chicken and Vegetables Ramen

This Slow Cooker Chicken and Vegetables Ramen transforms a couple of ramen packs into a big-batch dinner with tender chicken and fresh vegetables.

Cuisine Asian

Equipment

Ingredients

  • 1½ lb. chicken breasts 680g, (2 breasts) $4.00*
  • 8 oz. mushrooms cleaned and sliced, (227g) $1.94
  • 1 small onion sliced thinly, (2 cups, 225g) $0.62
  • 1 red bell pepper sliced thinly, (1 cup, 100g) $1.48

Instructions

  • Gather and prepare all ingredients.
  • Place the chicken, mushrooms, onions, red bell pepper, garlic, ginger, chicken broth, soy sauce, rice vinegar, toasted sesame oil, sriracha, and brown sugar in the crockpot. Fold all the ingredients together to combine.
  • Place the lid on and cook on high for 3 hours.
  • After 2 hours and 45 minutes, remove the chicken from the crock pot and place it in a medium-sized bowl. Using two forks, pull the chicken into bite-sized pieces.
  • Open the packs of ramen and discard the flavor packets. Place the ramen noodles in the crockpot and top with the chicken to submerge it in the broth. Continue cooking for the last 15 minutes.
  • Turn off the slow cooker, stir everything together, and top the ramen with sliced green onions and your favorite toppings. Enjoy!

Notes

*I tested this recipe with both chicken breasts and chicken thighs (boneless & skinless). Both work great with no adjustments needed, so use what you’ve got! Always thaw frozen chicken before adding it to the slow cooker to ensure it cooks safely and evenly.
**I like to use Better Than Bouillon for my chicken broth to keep costs low.
***If you’re sensitive to salt, use a low-sodium soy sauce and taste before adding any extra seasoning.
You can adjust the seasoning to your preference: Add more or less sriracha to control the spice, use less soy sauce (or a low-sodium option) if you don’t love a salty broth, or add more brown sugar if you want it sweeter.

how to make Slow Cooker Chicken and Vegetables Ramen Step-by-Step Photos

Gather all of your ingredients.

Build the broth: Add 1½ lb. chicken breasts, 8 oz. sliced mushrooms, 1 sliced onion, 1 sliced red bell pepper, 2 minced garlic cloves, and 2 tsp minced fresh ginger to your slow cooker. Pour in 3 cups chicken broth, 1 cup soy sauce, ½ cup rice vinegar, 1 Tbsp toasted sesame oil, 1 Tbsp sriracha, and 1 Tbsp brown sugar. Gently stir everything together to coat the vegetables and dissolve the sugar.

Slow cook until the chicken is tender: Cover with the lid and cook on HIGH for 3 hours. The vegetables will soften, the broth will become deeply flavorful, and the chicken should be cooked through and easy to shred. If you’re unsure, check the thickest part of the chicken with an instant-read thermometer. It should register 165°F.

Shred the chicken: After 2 hours and 45 minutes, transfer the chicken breasts to a medium bowl. Use two forks to shred the chicken into bite-sized pieces.

Cook the ramen: Open 2 packs ramen noodles and discard the seasoning packets. Add the noodle blocks to the slow cooker, gently pressing them into the broth.

Add the shredded chicken back to the slow cooker on top of the noodles. Cover and cook for the final 15 minutes. The noodles should be tender but still hold their shape.

Garnish and serve: Give everything a good stir so the chicken, vegetables, and noodles are evenly distributed throughout the broth. Divide between bowls and top with 2 sliced green onions and any additional toppings you like (optional). Serve your crockpot chicken and vegetable ramen while it’s piping hot. Enjoy!

Serving Suggestions

I like topping my ramen with a soy-marinated egg and a sprinkle of sesame seeds, as seen in the photos here. A soy-marinated egg is simply a soft-boiled egg left to soak in a soy sauce mixture made with many of the same ingredients already used in this recipe. You can see exactly how we make them in this video on our YouTube channel! Lime wedges, jalapeño slices, seaweed, corn, chili oil, cilantro, and our easy fermented vegetables are also delicious toppings.

This slow cooker chicken ramen also pairs nicely with our Thai cucumber salad or sesame slaw if you want something fresh and crunchy on the side.

Storage & Reheating

Store any leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3-4 days. If you’re planning ahead, I recommend storing the broth and shredded chicken together without the noodles, then cooking fresh packs of ramen when reheating. But if everything is already mixed together, don’t worry! It’ll still taste delicious. Just note the noodles will soak up some of the broth and soften a bit over time.

Reheating

Reheat individual portions gently on the stovetop over medium-low heat or in the microwave until steaming hot. If the noodles have soaked up some of the broth, stir in a splash of water or chicken broth to loosen everything back up.

If you stored the broth and chicken only, bring them to a gentle simmer, then add the fresh blocks of ramen and cook for 2-3 minutes before serving.

Freezing

For the best results, freeze just the broth and shredded chicken in a freezer-safe container for up to 3 months. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator (or use the defrost function on your microwave). Then reheat the broth on the stovetop and cook the fresh blocks of ramen directly in the hot broth before serving.

You can also freeze the noodles with the broth, but expect them to be a little softer after thawing and reheating!
